title: Holy, holy, holy
hookLine: Isaiah sees the seraphim calling: holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:1–3)
carry: taken apart, then put back together

cards: Isaiah dates his vision by a king's death. In the King James words: "In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple."
A king has died, and in the temple Isaiah sees something that fills the room past its edges: the hem of a robe so vast it pours through the whole building.
Above the throne stand the seraphim, calling one word to each other, three times over.

teach.h: EVEN THE SERAPHIM COVER THEIR FACES.
teach.b: First, the seraphim. The text describes them carefully: "each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly." Even these beings cover their faces.
Awe, in Isaiah, isn't staring. It's knowing you can't quite look.
Second, the call: "And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts". Three times, back and forth, as if once couldn't hold it. In Hebrew the word is qadosh.
Jewish prayer takes up these words in the Kedushah, and Christian worship sings them in the Sanctus.
Third, the half of the line that's easy to miss: "the whole earth is full of his glory." The holiness isn't kept inside the temple.

It spills out to the edges of the world, so the street outside, the market, the field, a kitchen, could all be places where that glory sits. Fourth, the human answer. Isaiah doesn't say how wonderful.

He says: "Woe is me! for I am undone". Undone: in the old English sense, ruined, come apart. In the story, one of the seraphim flies to him with a live coal from the altar, touches his lips, and his sin is purged.
Awe takes him apart before it puts him back together.
And the seraphim's line leaves a question: what would it be like to call one ordinary thing holy, and mean it?

how: Jews say the seraphim's words in the Kedushah, part of the repeated Amidah prayer, and Christians sing them in the Sanctus at the Eucharist; both come from Isaiah 6:3.

games.q: you're Isaiah, in the temple, and the whole room is full of the vision. what do you say?
o: woe is me, I am undone.
games.why: "woe is me! for I am undone." then one of the seraphim touches his lips with a live coal from the altar.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing in reach, a cup, a key, your own hand, and rest your eyes on it: where it came from, who made it, what it has held.
Then say one word over it, quietly or inside: holy, not because it's special, but because the seraphim said the whole earth is full.
If you pray, you can say their words themselves; if the word feels too big, just look a little longer.

wordCard.voice: Holy. In Hebrew, qadosh: the word the seraphim call to each other three times in Isaiah's vision, with the whole earth full of glory. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: holy. the seraphim call it three times in Isaiah 6:3.

carryVoice: Your line: taken apart, then put back together. Woe is me came first; the live coal came after. See you tomorrow.
